BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, what a game is. Twenty-two terms for what makes something a game, what the player does and feels, and how a game gets made. The exact term lets you tell a team, or an AI coding agent, precisely what to change.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for bear. Newcomers often say a game is any activity with a goal. It is not. A serial race has a goal, opposition, and rules, and it is still not a game because the player makes no decisions. A game needs all four. This film goes through the terms group by group, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Seven labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Video only, the term comes from a video lecture and is not in the course text or on the term list. Computed, the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map, 22 terms about what a game is in four groups. The first group asks whether an activity is a game at all, with the terms game, goal, opposition, decisions, rules, and house rules.

B0102.heard: The second group is what the player does, mechanic, player verb, core mechanic, and core loop. These terms name the actions and the one action the player repeats most.

B0103.heard: The third group is what the player feels, types of fun, target experience, thematic feel, movement pattern and appeal. These terms name the experience that the actions add up to.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is how it gets made. Space, components, art, design and engineering, prototype, play testing, clear progress and climactic arc. These terms name what the team builds, tests and shapes.

B0201.heard: A table scores three activities against the four parts of a game. The first column is goal, the objective the player works toward what you are trying to reach. Tennis has won and so does a serial race. Just eating cereal has none. For example, in a platformer level the goal is the flag at the far end. The spikes on the way are not the goal. They stand in the way.

B0202.heard: The second column is opposition, the obstacles the player must overcome. Opposition makes a game fun and it can also frustrate. Tennis has an opponent across the net and a serial race has the other racers. Eating serial has nothing in the way. For example, an enemy that patrols back and forth on a narrow platform is opposition. The player wants the flag and the enemy stands in the way.

B0203.heard: The third column is decisions the ways the player can get past the opposition. Tennis has them such as where to hit the ball. The serial race gets a red cross because all eraser can do is eat faster. For example, when a patrolling enemy blocks the path, the player can jump over it, wait for it to turn around or take a higher platform. Those are decisions.

B0204.heard: The last column is rules, the framework that limits and governs the whole experience. A game is an activity that has all four parts. Tennis scores for a four are a game, eating cereal scores 0-4. The cereal race scores 3-4 with no decisions yet. For example, a level with a flag to reach, spikes in the way, two routes to choose between, and a rule that spikes restart the level has all four so it is a game.

B0301.heard: Three small boards each with one piece in the middle. Rules limit what the player may choose, and they are set for everyone who plays. With no rules, the piece has eight legal moves. Add one rule, no diagonal moves, and only four are left. For example, a platformer rule that the player may jump only while standing on the ground, removes every jump in midair for every player.

B0302.heard: The third board shows house rules, rules a group changes for its own table. This group adds one no backing up and the choice list shrinks from 8 moves to 5. A house rule is still a rule and it changes how the game plays. For example, friends playing your platformer agree to finish a level without touching a single coin. The game allows coins and their table does not.

B0401.heard: A row of 40 actions from one minute of play in a simulated run. A mechanic is a rule-governed action in the game. A player verb is an action the player can take named as a verb, such as jump or shoot. The look alike is a component, an object, a noun. For example, in Walker's three-dimensional platformer, a robot moves, jumps, collects coins and shoots. Jump is a player verb and jump with its rules attached, such as how high it rises is a mechanic.

B0402.heard: Now the 40 actions are counted by verb. The core mechanic is the action players do over and over again. In this simulated minute, jump comes up 23 times out of 40, 57% of the actions. Shoot comes 10 times, run 5 and collect 2. For example, in a platformer where most of every level is crossing gaps, jump is the core mechanic, so it is the action to tune and test first.

B0403.heard: A circle appears and a dot travels around it twice. The core loop is the repeated moment to moment cycle the player enjoys. If the cycle goes run, then jump, then collect, then shoot, and back to run. The core mechanic is one action. The core loop is the whole cycle the actions make. For example, in a coin platformer, the loop is run to a ledge, jump the gap, grab the coin, and run on to the next ledge.

B0501.heard: A plain cube sits on a grid, there is no art yet so nothing says what it is. Thematic feel is the idea that mechanics alone can set the tone. What a thing does tells the player what it is before it looks like anything. The lookalike is art, what the thing looks like. For example, a grey placeholder square that follows the player and snaps at them when it gets near already feels like a hungry enemy.

B0502.heard: Now add one rule, the cube hurts the cells around it then disappears. In this computed picture it hits the eight cells around its own square. Nobody drew a fuse yet the player sees a bomb. That is thematic feel at work, the rule alone says what the thing is. For example, a placeholder block that holds the player for a moment and then sinks away feels like a crumbling platform before any art is made.

B0503.heard: Widen the blast to two cells in every direction and the 24 cells around it square are hit. Same cube, same lack of art, but the player now feels more danger and more power. One number and one rule change the feeling, so art and mechanics must tell the same story. For example, if an enemy is drawn as a tiny harmless mouse but its attack covers half the screen, the look and the rule disagree and the player feels cheated.

B0504.heard: The grid gives way to three enemy paths. Movement pattern means that how a character moves gives it personality. The same cube goes straight forward, hops or waves from side to side and becomes three different creatures. A hop says frog and a wave says snake. For example, an enemy box in a platformer that drops from the ceiling and climbs back up on a thread feels like a spider, with no spider art at all.

B0601.heard: A six-sided radar chart with one kind of fun on each corner. Types of fun says the word fun is too vague to build with. Name the kind, fantasy, thrill, fellowship, mastery, exploration, or creativity. In this made-up profile, the game reaches far toward mastery and only a little toward the rest. For example, a hidden room behind a breakable wall offers exploration, while a hard run of jumps that takes practice offers mastery.

B0602.heard: Mastery is now marked in red. A target experience is the one specific experience everyone on the team aims at. It is one chosen kind of fun where plain fun is too vague to build or test. In this made up profile, Mastery takes 42% of the whole. For example, a team picks Mastery as the target for its platformer. So every new level is judged by one question. Does it reward practice?

B0603.heard: Two players score the same game. Appeal is the pull to keep playing and it differs by game and by player. Here Appeal adds up what each player wants times with the game offers. Player A who wants mastery scores this made up game 29. Player B who wants fantasy scores at 11. For example, a hard platformer with little story keeps a player who loves practice and loses a player who came for a world to escape into.

B0701.heard: Three arrows leave one point. Art, design and engineering depend on each other, and they do best when all three aim at the same target experience. Here they spread 73 degrees apart. Art made a stealth assassin, design made a tank, and engineering built a third thing. Design is rules and mechanics what the player can do. Art is look and sound. For example, a nimble ninja sprite given a slow, heavy jump is art and design pulling apart.

B0702.heard: The arrows swing together until the angle between them is zero. The target experience was agreed first, so the three disciplines now set each other up for easy wins. For example, a team agrees on a quick nimble hero. Art draws a light, lean sprite, design gives it a fast, short jump, and engineering makes the controls answer the instant a key goes down.

B0801.heard: A room seen from above with a lit zone and a ring of sound and nothing in it yet. Space is the look, sound, lighting and physical setting of a game. It sets the mood and it limits which characters and actions fit. The counter reads zero components. For example, a dark cave level with echoing drips and one shaft of light is space. It suits a careful explorer far better than a racing car.

B0802.heard: Four objects appear in the room, a character, a key, a door, and a vehicle. Components are the objects in the space that players use or meet, such as characters, weapons and vehicles. Space is the setting, and components are the things inside it. Take the space away, and they have nowhere to be. For example, in a cave level, the coins, the spikes, the bats, and the player character are components, and the cave itself is the space.

B0901.heard: Two bars compare what it costs to find out whether a game is fun. A prototype is a simplified version made first to test whether the idea has appeal. In this made-up example, the prototype with the core action only takes one week, and the full game with art and levels takes 40 weeks. For example, before modeling any character in Blender, a team builds the jump with gray boxes in Go-Doh and plays it to see whether jumping alone is fun.

B0902.heard: The curve is the gap to the intended design. Play testing means letting players challenge the design so it can be revisited and improved. A prototype asks once whether the idea has appeal while play testing checks the design round by round. In this made-up example, each round removes 40% of what is left, so after 6 rounds the gap is 5 of 100. For example, testers keep missing a hidden ledge, so you add a coin trail toward it and test again.

B1001.heard: A bar fills from left to right, a payload moving toward the goal with a checkpoint at 50%. Clear progress means the player can see how near they are to the goal. At the checkpoint, you and the other team both know how far is left. Without it, you cannot tell if you are doing well. For example, a small map at the top of the screen that shows the player's dot moving toward the flag gives clear progress.

B1002.heard: Now a curve of tension against progress. Climactic arc means difficulty and tension build toward the goal's resolution. In this made-up curve, tension is 0.34 at halfway and 0.80 at 90%. Progress is how far you are, and tension is how hard it feels right now. For example, a level that starts with wide, easy gaps and ends with narrow jumps over spikes just before the flag has a climactic arc.

B1101.heard: Look alike pairs side by side. On the left goal in its other sense, the experience what the player should feel and do. On the right tactic, the choices and rules that deliver it. For example, the goal is a tense escape, and a countdown timer is a tactic.

B1102.heard: Pair 2, a mechanic is an action, a verb that repeats like the dot that keeps jumping. A component is an object, a noun in the space like the block that just sits there. Jumping is a mechanic and a coin is a component.

B1103.heard: Pair 3 rules are the same for everyone. With no diagonals the piece has 4 legal moves. House rules are one group's change to them. With no backing up it is 5. Both limit what the player can choose.

B1104.heard: Pair 4, a prototype is one small test of the idea, here a single week. Play testing is repeated rounds that refine the design and the gap shrinks each round. One asks whether the idea has appeal. The other keeps improving it.

B1201.heard: Vague requests sit beside exact instructions and the numbers are examples. Make it more fun becomes target experience mastery and add one skill based decision every 10 seconds. The chart shows 6 decisions in 60 seconds, 1 every 10.

B1202.heard: It feels pointless becomes show progress with a checkpoint at 50% and at 75% of the level. As the bar fills, the player passes both marks and can see how far is left.

B1203.heard: Make the boss tense becomes raise tension toward the end. The boss attacks 1.5 times faster below 25% health. On the chart, the attack rate jumps from 1.0 to 1.5 at that point.

B1204.heard: I died and don't know why it becomes telegraph the attack with a wind up of half a second before the damage, to telegraph means to show it coming. The dot crosses the gray wind up bar to the red hit so the player gets half a second of warning.

B1205.heard: The game feels unfair becomes be consistent, the same wind up and the same damage 10 every time. On the chart, random hits have a spread of 10.1, consistent hits have a spread of 0 so the player can learn what to expect.

B1301.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you call a design done. First, does it have a goal, opposition, decisions, and rules? If one is missing, it is not yet a game.

B1302.heard: Second, can you name the player verb and the core mechanic? The one action the player repeats more than any other.

B1303.heard: Third, which one kind of fun are you aiming at? Name it such as mastery, thrill, or exploration, and make it the target experience.

B1304.heard: Fourth, do art, design, and engineering all aim at that target. If the look, the rules, and the code point different ways, the game feels wrong to play.

B1305.heard: Fifth can the player see progress toward the goal through a checkpoint, a bar, or a map, so they can tell whether they are doing well.

B1306.heard: 6. Did you prototype and play test before adding more? Then say it exactly. Not make it more fun, but aim at mastery.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap, a game needs a goal, opposition, decisions and rules, all four of them. A house rule is still a rule, one group's own change to the rules. The core mechanic is the action repeated most and the core loop is the cycle. What a thing does and how it moves tells the player what it is. Name one target experience because plain fun is too vague to build or test. A prototype tests the idea and play testing refines the design round by round.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on game design terms with short game making cases one at a time. Use goal, opposition, decisions, house rules, mechanic, component, core mechanic, core loop, target experience and play testing. For each case I must name the exact term and say why it's look-alike does not fit. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me whether I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms what a game is at Nick Bear Brown.
